description: We are OrbitGuardians, a multidisciplinary team comprising a mathematician, a machine learning engineer, a chemist, and a developer growing her expertise in machine learning. We combine mathematical modelling, scientific thinking, and software development to explore challenges in astronaut health. Through Space-Twin, we aim to transform complex health data into clear, interactive insights that support astronaut well-being during long-duration space missions.
summary:
Space-Twin reimagines astronaut healthcare through an intelligence digital twin that transforms fragmented mission data into an intelligent, interactive health companion. Instead of viewing isolated metrics, astronauts and mission teams can visualize how cardiovascular health, musculoskeletal condition, cognitive performance, sleep, and environmental factors evolve together throughout a mission, and explore how changes in exercise or sleep could influence future wellbeing.
Built with a React and Three.js immersive interface powered by a Python FastAPI backend, Space-Twin combines advanced visualization with experimental AI capabilities, including pose estimation, machine-learning-based anomaly detection, public NASA data integration, and an AI mission assistant. Together, these technologies create a unified platform for exploring crew health in real time.
As humanity prepares for longer missions to the Moon and Mars, proactive health monitoring will become increasingly important. Space-Twin demonstrates how AI and digital twin technology could help mission teams move beyond reactive monitoring toward predictive, personalized insights. While the current prototype uses synthetic data and is not a validated medical device, it presents a compelling vision for the future of space medicine.
details:
Space-Twin is an interactive digital health twin that brings astronaut health indicators, mission conditions, and exploratory simulations into a single visual environment. Instead of viewing health data as separate measurements, Space-Twin creates a connected picture of crew wellbeing by combining cardiovascular, musculoskeletal, cognitive, sleep, well-being, and environmental factors into an evolving mission profile.

Through an immersive dashboard, users can explore health trends, review status indicators, and run “what-if” scenarios to examine how changes in exercise or sleep routines may influence a simulated astronaut twin over time. This approach supports a shift from simply monitoring astronaut health toward understanding patterns, relationships, and possible future outcomes during long-duration missions.

The prototype includes experimental computer vision tools that estimate body landmarks from images using Ultralytics YOLO26n-pose and identify generic visual anomalies using a scikit-learn Isolation Forest trained on reference images. These features are designed as exploratory tools that provide additional context for human review, not as diagnostic systems or fitness-for-duty assessments. Space-Twin also incorporates public NASA resources and an optional mission assistant to connect health exploration with broader mission information.

The platform was developed using React, JavaScript, Vite, and Three.js for the interactive interface, with a backend built using Python, FastAPI, and Uvicorn. SQLite manages research records, while NumPy, Pillow, and scikit-learn support data processing and machine-learning experiments. NASA APIs and optional Groq and Roboflow integrations extend the prototype with additional mission context and services.

The creative aspect of Space-Twin is the combination of human-centered visualization, digital twin concepts, scenario exploration, and mission context into one experience. Rather than presenting astronauts with disconnected streams of information, it creates a shared environment where crews and ground teams can explore how different factors interact.

The intended impact is to demonstrate how future space missions could use digital twins to support communication, planning, and health awareness when astronauts operate far from Earth. Throughout development, the team considered data privacy, uncertainty, responsible use of experimental models, and the limitations of synthetic data. The current prototype is a research concept using simulated readings and illustrative assumptions; it is not a validated medical system.
